Moving Science Towards Operational Sustainability: The 
Use of Geospatial Decision Support Systems

1   |   Introduction
The demands on our landscapes increasingly conflict with each 
other (e.g., the transition to sustainable agriculture versus the 
expansion of urban areas). We must address increasing land 
degradation problems (e.g., erosion, loss of soil fertility and bio-
diversity, floods, pollution) and the imperative to move toward 
land use sustainability. Making decisions to meet these diverse 
requirements and solve problems is often highly complex and 
challenging. Similar issues are evident in the implementation 
of multiscale land policies at global (e.g., SDGs), European 
(e.g., CAP), national (e.g., climate change adaptation plans 
in EU Member States), regional (e.g., implementation of the 
EU Nitrates Directive), and local (e.g., urban planning) levels. 
There is a need to bridge the knowledge gap between decision-­
makers, who require operational support to implement policies 
and actions toward land use sustainability, and the research 
community.
The development of Decision Support Systems (DSS), particu-
larly geoSpatial Decision Support Systems (S-­DSS) including 
Digital Twin-­based tools, offers a promising avenue to address 
these complex challenges. Over the past decade, advancements 
in S-­DSS were driven by progress in land management sciences, 
databases, modelling, datacube technologies, high-­performance 
computing (HPC), Earth Observation (EO), artificial intelligence 
(AI), WebGIS facilities, and Geospatial Cyberinfrastructure. 
Together, these advancements have significantly enhanced the 
connection between land resource science and practical, opera-
tional land management.
1.1   |   Outline
In this scenario, the current LDD special issue collects research 
papers on advanced approaches and methodologies in land-­
based Spatial Decision Support Systems (S-­DSS), aiming to 
address whether S-­DSS can effectively handle the complexity 
of the challenges mentioned above and facilitate the transition 
toward sustainable land and soil use.
The focus is to cover the following items: (i) the diversity of ap-
proaches, both from a methodological and end-­user perspective, 
using multidisciplinary and multifunctional strategies in view 
of the development of Decision Support Systems, (ii) the imple-
mentation of S-­DSS to promote sustainable land uses in vari-
ous sectors such as agriculture, forestry, urban planning, land 
revitalization, climate change, and environmental and human 
health.
This special issue aims to test the feasibility of S-­DSS in facili-
tating a scientific paradigm shift in working with the physical 
landscape by overcoming the current fragmentation of the many 
separate applied research approaches toward the common ob-
jective of sustainable land planning and management. More spe-
cifically, S-­DSS promise to integrate geospatial knowledge that 
helps bridge the gap between scientists working on landscape 
research and end-­users.
This special issue, with a specific focus on sustainable land man-
agement, aligns well with the core focus of Land Degradation 
and Development. It aims to advance the field by exploring

1.2   |   A Short Overview on Geospatial Decision 
Support Systems (S-­DSS)
Geospatial Decision Support Systems (S-­DSS) are decision sup-
port systems that incorporate geospatial information, making 
them particularly valuable for addressing land-­based issues such 
as land planning and management. Their applications span var-
ious sectors, including agriculture, forestry, environmental pro-
tection, and urban planning.
These S-­DSS systems have a history marked by both successes 
and failures (e.g., Geertman and Stillwell 2009).
To analyze the development of these S-­DSS systems across differ-
ent scientific domains from the 1990s onward, we have employed 
a citation-­mapping analysis following the methods by Trujillo and 
Long (2018). Figure 1 shows that most of the advancements have 
taken place in the last decade, and it is evident—though expected—
that there are very diverse, unconnected clusters. Besides urban 
transport and waste management, there are clusters for “Land Use 
Policies & Ecosystem Services” and “Rural Development.” These 
last two themes are particularly relevant to this special issue.
A deeper insight into the use of S-­DSS systems within the “soil 
science” domain is shown in Figure 2. It can be observed that 
the majority of developments in this area have occurred in the 
last decade. Notably, there are four distinct clusters—land use 
policy, soil sealing, modelling, and agriculture—that again 
do not interact with each other. These clusters appear to have 
evolved independently, each driven by different objectives.
The new generation of S-­DSS makes it possible to link these clus-
ters, on the basis that the solutions to be applied to the sustainable 
management of territories must not be mono-­disciplinary but 
rather have to be trans-­disciplinary and must cover multiscale 
and multistakeholder needs.
1.3   |   The Content of This Special Issue
This Special Issue assembles 15 papers that cover a broad 
spectrum of topics, from weed control to climate change, 
all analyzed through the perspective of developing S-­DSSs. 
Approximately, 60% of the papers refer to actual S-­DSS appli-
cations, while the other half focus on preliminary steps, such 
as analyzing environmental and land features relevant for de-
veloping DSS or S-­DSS. Below, we provide detailed insight into 
these contributions.
1.3.1   |   Papers From the Landsupport S-­DSS Project
Approximately 45% of the submitted papers are related to the 
EU Horizon 2020 project named LANDSUPPORT (www.​lands​
upport.​eu), funded by the European Commission (Call RUR-­
03-­2017), and its connected final international conference. The 
LANDSUPPORT project aims to develop a web-­based, free, 
open-­access GeoSpatial Decision Support System (S-­DSS) to 
support sustainable agriculture and forestry, evaluate land-­use 
trade-­offs, and contribute to land-­use policy development and 
implementation in Europe. The project developed a comprehen-
sive set of operational, transdisciplinary S-­DSS tools based on 
a smart Geospatial CyberInfrastructure (GCI) across different 
geographical and governance scales, ensuring substantial trans-
ferability across diverse physical, socio-­economic, and cultural 
settings. The papers describe the scientific approaches and re-
sults in developing these operational tools. Terribile et al. (2024) 
detail the central concept and results of developing a multiscale, 
multistakeholder, and transdisciplinary S-­DSS, demonstrat-
ing that reconciling agriculture and the environment is feasi-
ble with appropriate DSS tools. Manna et al. (2024) showcase 
an S-­DSS tool used to quantify land degradation across the EU,

fulfilling SDG 15.3 requirements. Baumann et al. (2024) address 
the critical issue of database architecture (datacube technology) 
necessary for implementing high-­performance S-­DSS systems. 
Bonfante et al. (2024) present an operational S-­DSS tool devel-
oped to estimate the impact of climate change at various NUTS 
levels (e.g., municipalities to countries) across the EU, with addi-
tional focus on crop adaptability in Italy. Mileti et al. (2024) pro-
duce a biodiversity tool implementing the EU Habitat Directive 
at the regional level (Campania region in Italy) while Bancheri 
et  al.  (2024) demonstrate a tool based on process-­based (crop 
growth) modelling implemented in an S-­DSS, evaluating agri-
cultural best practices in real-­time based on site-­specific pedo-
climatic information. Finally, Stankovics et al. (2024) highlight 
the critical importance of stakeholder engagement in developing 
successful S-­DSS systems.
1.3.2   |   Other Papers on DSS
Two papers focus on DSS applied to multi-­criteria decision sup-
port systems in aquaculture (Dharani Shrree et al. 2024) and on 
the prediction of Festuca ovina for the restoration of degraded 
lands (Saffariha et al. 2023).
1.3.3   |   Other Papers Dealing With More Basic Issues 
Relevant in View of Future DSS and SDSS Needs
The remaining 40% of contributions cover preliminary research 
relevant to S-­DSS development, including Spatiotemporal evo-
lution and driving mechanisms of slope cultivated land (Yu, Li 
et al. 2024), Land pressure evaluation through the lens of the 
production-­living-­ecology framework (Yu, Chen et al. 2024), A 
framework for quantifying and integrating green development 
of cultivated land in China, using an Adaptability-­Vitality-­
Resistance (AVR) perspective (Niu et al. 2024), Spatial variabil-
ity of soil organic carbon in China's terrestrial ecosystems (Li 
et al. 2024), Optimization strategies for ecological security pat-
terns (Wei et al. 2024), Risk assessment in a contaminated area 
(Mondaca et al. 2024).
2   |   Conclusion
This special issue of Land Degradation & Development reveals 
a dynamic and evolving landscape of research in the field of 
Spatial Decision Support Systems (S-­DSS). It offers a compelling 
overview of the latest advancements in methodologies, showcas-
ing the development of sophisticated tools designed to address 
complex land management challenges. A key theme emerging 
from the collected papers is the necessity of transdisciplinary 
collaboration. The development of effective S-­DSS requires inte-
grating expertise from various scientific domains, including soil 
science, environmental science, computer science, and social 
science. This collaborative approach ensures that S-­DSS tools 
are not only scientifically sound but also address the practical 
needs of stakeholders and policymakers.
Furthermore, the special issue emphasizes the importance of 
making these tools accessible to a wider audience. Several pa-
pers present freely available, web-­based S-­DSS tools, demon-
strating a commitment to open access and knowledge sharing. 
This approach facilitates broader adoption of S-­DSS by land 
managers, researchers, and policymakers, ultimately promoting 
more sustainable land use practices.
Looking ahead, the insights presented in this special issue on 
advanced approaches and methodologies in land-­based Spatial 
Decision Support Systems (S-­DSS) underscore the potential of 
S-­DSS to revolutionize land management practices. By foster-
ing collaboration between scientists and end-­users, S-­DSS can 
empower informed decision-­making, bridge the gap between 
research and application, and promote a more sustainable fu-
ture for our lands. The development and widespread adoption of 
S-­DSS are crucial steps toward addressing the complex environ-
mental challenges facing our world today.
